items.title: IBM's most advanced quantum computer unveiled at UChicago's Hyde Park Labs
items.summary: IBM switched on its most advanced quantum computer in Hyde Park, on Chicago's South Side. It is the first IBM quantum computer in Illinois. Scientists and companies will use it to test ideas like better drug discovery and a more efficient power grid. Later it is planned to move to the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park.
items.whyItMattersForChicago: The machine is on the South Side. IBM says it is helping City Colleges of Chicago design an apprenticeship program. IBM has promised to hire one-third of the qualified graduates.

items.title: Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park's $20,000 donation lets school craft quantum lab
items.summary: PsiQuantum, the main company moving into the quantum park, gave $20,000 to St. Francis de Sales High School in South Chicago. The money pays for a new science lab where students can do hands-on work. The school plans to share what it gets with other nearby schools.
items.whyItMattersForChicago: This is a real lab built for South Side students, a few miles from the park where quantum jobs are expected.

items.title: PsiQuantum and AMD Expand Partnership with Equity Investment to Co-Design Utility-Scale Quantum Infrastructure
items.summary: Two tech companies, PsiQuantum and AMD, are teaming up more closely to design the regular computers and the quantum computers that would have to work side by side. AMD plans to invest money in PsiQuantum. Both companies say they are looking at having a joint presence in Chicago.
items.whyItMattersForChicago: PsiQuantum is the anchor tenant of the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park, which is being built on the former South Works steel site.

items.title: Aaron Fluitt joins the Chicago Quantum Exchange as CEO
items.summary: The Chicago Quantum Exchange is a group of more than 70 members and partners, including universities, labs and companies, that work together on quantum technology. It has a new CEO, Aaron Fluitt, who used to work at Argonne National Laboratory and PsiQuantum. He says his goals include building the supply chain for quantum equipment and training more people for quantum jobs.
items.whyItMattersForChicago: Training and talent development for quantum jobs is on the new CEO's list of priorities for the Chicago region.

items.title: UChicago to collaborate with Tohoku University to bolster quantum research and education
items.summary: The University of Chicago's Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering and Tohoku University in Japan will work together for an initial five years. They will share lab space and equipment, and students and teachers can visit each other's schools. A goal is to train more quantum engineers in both countries.
items.whyItMattersForChicago: Chicago-area universities are adding student exchanges and job training in quantum. That is worth a look when you pick a college.

items.title: Light-activated molecules in porous crystals show potential for quantum chemical sensing
items.summary: A team from the University of Tokyo and Northwestern University made special pairs of molecules inside a sponge-like crystal. When light hits them, their tiny magnetic spins line up, and the spins change when certain chemicals are nearby. This could lead to sensors that work like a "quantum nose."
items.whyItMattersForChicago: A Northwestern chemist helped lead this team. So Chicago-area scientists work on quantum sensors, not only quantum computers.

items.title: Made to sense dark matter, quantum control kit becomes something more
items.summary: Fermilab built QICK, a briefcase-sized, open-source kit that helps scientists run quantum experiments. It costs about one-tenth as much as similar systems. Companies and labs now use it with many kinds of qubits, and a Department of Energy program is helping it reach more users.
items.whyItMattersForChicago: Fermilab, a national lab near Chicago, designs and manages this tool. So some quantum lab equipment is built close to home.

items.title: Quantinuum Breaks Error-Correction World Record by 10x, Validating its Leading Path to Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing by 2029
items.summary: Quantum computers make mistakes, so scientists use error correction to catch and fix them. The company Quantinuum says its Helios machine made only about five errors per million steps after correction, ten times better than its own record from the month before. This is a company announcement, so other scientists will want to check it.
items.whyItMattersForChicago: Fixing errors is key to building useful quantum computers. PsiQuantum, the park's anchor company, says its goal is a fault-tolerant machine.

items.title: NIST Report Provides Guidelines for Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards
items.summary: Future quantum computers might be able to break some of the codes that protect private information online. A U.S. government agency called NIST published a plan for moving to new codes that quantum computers cannot easily break. The plan tells organizations which older codes to stop using and when.
items.whyItMattersForChicago: Computer security teams everywhere, including Chicago employers, will need to switch to new encryption. That creates cybersecurity jobs.

items.title: Chip-based laser cooling could ease quantum computing bottleneck
items.summary: Some quantum computers hold single atoms in place and have to cool them down with lasers before each step. Cornell researchers built the lasers into a tiny chip and cooled an atom about three times faster than a regular setup. Faster cooling could help future machines grow larger.

items.title: Research advances quantum computing that harnesses speed of light
items.summary: Some quantum computers use single particles of light, called photons, as their qubits. Engineers at Purdue University describe possible fixes for several problems in the way. One is a way to make single photons on a silicon nitride chip at room temperature. Challenges remain, but light-based machines could run without the super-cold fridges that many quantum computers need.
items.whyItMattersForChicago: PsiQuantum, the park's anchor company, builds quantum computers from particles of light. So progress on light-based chips is part of that story.
